title: Attention as Frustrated Synchronization
abstract: A network of oscillators that synchronizes perfectly computes nothing further, so an attention architecture built from synchronization must locate its computation in structured departures from agreement. We introduce the Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN), whose token states are phases on a torus and whose entire value pathway is one learned complex coupling kernel over harmonics and a one-step delay. Each component of the kernel is a frustration in the sense of the synchronization literature. The complex phases are static Kuramoto-Sakaguchi frustration angles, the signed harmonics are repulsive Daido components, and the delay term, which couples each token to the successors of the tokens it attends to, is algebraically identical to Kuramoto-Sakaguchi coupling whose frustration angle is the data's own transition, so next-token prediction is implemented as synchronization frustrated by the data. At matched one-million-parameter and training budgets on character-level text and code, the FSN's validation loss is below a tuned RoPE-SwiGLU transformer's at every epoch measured, and the comparison survives training the baseline to convergence: every thirty-epoch enwik8 seed finishes below the transformer's converged fifty-epoch loss of 1.611, and the FSN's completed fifty-epoch runs converge to 1.5953 +/- 0.0014. A variant with every feed-forward block replaced by mean-field coupling to learned collective modes, leaving no multilayer perceptron in the stack, tracks the transformer. On natural text the unfrustrated base layer falls behind the converged transformer at every copy depth, worst on long-range copy events; the kernel reverses the deficit at every depth of four and beyond. Headline comparisons are at the one-million-parameter scale; a scale ladder is complete through four million parameters with the advantage persisting, and remaining arms are marked as in progress.
summary: This paper proposes the Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN), an attention mechanism that reinterprets context processing as frustrated synchronization among coupled oscillators. By replacing standard consensus mechanisms with dynamics incorporating data-driven frustration and delays, the FSN achieves state-of-the-art performance on character-level text and code benchmarks compared to transformers.
main_problem: The paper addresses how sequence prediction can be improved by modifying attention mechanisms from consensus-based retrieval to a process modeled by frustrated synchronization.
main_result: The proposed Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN) consistently outperforms tuned transformer baselines on character-level text and code corpora, especially when analyzing performance on long-range copy events.
method: It introduces the FSN, which models token state updates using a complex coupling kernel derived from coupled oscillators on a torus, incorporating frustration angles and data-dependent delays.
model_or_system: The core model is the Frustrated Synchronization Network (FSN), an oscillator-based attention layer replacing standard self-attention. It uses phases on a torus ($\mathbb{T}^k$) and models coupling via Kuramoto–Sakaguchi-like dynamics, where prediction is framed as synchronization frustrated by the data's transition.
key_observables: Validation loss (bits per character) on enwik8 and code corpora; performance margins analyzed across 'copy depth' bins ($\ell$); convergence rates over epochs.
important_parameters: One-million to eight-million parameters; copy depth $\ell$; frustration angles derived from data transitions ($\delta_u$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the failure of standard attention on long repetitions is due to its inability to capture non-periodic, accumulated 'winding information' present in the raw phase state.
figures_summary: Figures show per-token cross-entropy margins vs. copy depth bins, demonstrating the FSN's advantage where base layers fail (deep bins $\ge 4$). Other figures track loss vs. training time across parameter scales.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first defining the physical analogy of attention as synchronization, then introducing the FSN kernel structure (including harmonics and delay terms), presenting quantitative results showing superior performance over transformers on convergence and deep-copy tasks, and finally analyzing efficiency scaling with model size.
why_interesting: The explicit mapping of complex neural network dynamics onto established concepts from coupled oscillator theory (Kuramoto models) provides a novel physical interpretation for sequence modeling failures, particularly concerning long-range dependencies.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
